column2: The city of winds and oil fountains, where the ultra-modern Flame Towers are reflected in the Caspian Sea.
An ancient city built from pink tuff, where brandy flows freely and Mount Ararat is always in view—just across the border.
The capital of hospitality, where the number of khinkali you eat determines your status in the eyes of local winemakers.
A city of endless tea and eternal porridge, where the five o’clock rain arrives strictly on schedule.
Europe’s capital of techno, street art and döner kebabs, where the remnants of the Wall have become the ultimate tourist photo spot.
The heart of Spain, where siesta is not just a break but a sacred duty to do absolutely nothing in the middle of the workday.
Western Europe’s westernmost capital, where trams climb such steep hills that passengers instinctively start praying.
A musical capital where the aroma of classic coffee and strudel makes you forget the price of an opera ticket.
The city of a hundred spires and endless beer, where cobblestones are merciless to high heels and roast pork knuckle to diets.
A Polish capital risen from the ashes, where historic churches gaze at modern glass skyscrapers.
A city split by the Danube into Buda and Pest, where the best parties happen in ruins and the best relaxation in thermal baths.
The birthplace of democracy and olives, where modern Greeks take their time among the ancient ruins of the Parthenon.
A capital spread across 14 islands that gave the world IKEA, ABBA and Stockholm syndrome—the curious bond between captor and captive.
A city of Vikings and eye-watering prices, where a cup of coffee can cost as much as a small used car.
A capital with more saunas than cars, where the main pastime is silently contemplating the Baltic Sea.
The city where St.Patrick drove out the snakes to make room for endless pubs and lovers of dark stout.
The EU’s headquarters, famous for its officials, chocolates and a rather questionable little statue of a peeing boy.
A bicycle kingdom with more canals than Venice, where legal amusements leave tourists grinning foolishly.
Home of the Little Mermaid and hygge, where people manage to feel cozy even in an icy Baltic wind.
A capital of Art Nouveau and sprats, where it is easy to get lost in the Old Town after one too many glasses of local Black Balsam.
A city of Baroque architecture and the independent Republic of Užupis, where angels sit on rooftops and tourists sit in cozy cafés.
A medieval capital where the towers Long Hermann and Fat Margaret ensure that life moves at a thoroughly unhurried pace.
The Big Apple never sleeps because ambulance and fire-engine sirens roar around the clock.
A city of the White House and the Capitol, where three-piece suits and folders of compromising material are found in unreasonable quantities.
A windy city with a gangster past, where deep-dish pizza looks more like a pie and skyscrapers disappear into the clouds.
A sunny Florida paradise of fitness-model beaches and warm ocean water, where alligators occasionally wander into swimming pools.
A Canadian metropolis with the CN Tower that Hollywood constantly films as a stand-in for New York.
A Quebec wonder where people speak French, eat maple syrup and sincerely consider themselves more cultured than the rest of Canada.
A giant metropolis built on a dried-up Aztec lake, where spicy food can make you breathe fire.
A city of vintage cars, rum and cigars, where time stopped somewhere in the middle of the last century.
A city of endless carnival and tiny bikinis, majestically watched over by Christ the Redeemer with outstretched arms.
An airplane-shaped capital built in an empty field by Oscar Niemeyer, making it harder for officials to escape to the beach.
The birthplace of tango and steak, where passion boils in the streets and the architecture desperately tries to look Parisian.
A capital squeezed between the Andes and the Pacific, where earthquakes are simply a chance to check whether the furniture is sturdy.
South America’s culinary capital, serving the finest ceviche while the sun hides behind garúa fog for half the year.
A high-altitude metropolis under a permanent blanket of cloud, where coffee wakes you up and wall graffiti is recognized as official art.
A capital of endless summer, beautiful women and sky-high inflation, where banknotes are easier to use as wallpaper.
The capital of Peking duck and the Great Wall, where smog sometimes lets you see the sun and bicycle traffic obeys the laws of physics.
China’s New York, whose futuristic Pudong district looks as if it were designed by aliens from the 22nd century.
A financial hive clinging to the rocks, where property prices are heading for outer space and skyscrapers are built according to feng shui.
A neon anthill where robots serve sushi, trains run to the second and special subway staff push passengers into packed carriages.
Japan’s street-food and comedy capital, whose residents consider Tokyoites overly stiff and boring.
Japan’s cultural heart, with a thousand temples, geisha still wearing kimono and bamboo groves rustling in the wind.
The home of K-pop, TV dramas and sheet masks, where free Wi-Fi reaches even ancient royal palaces.
The world’s most closed-off capital, with flawless parades, monumental leaders’ statues and virtually no traffic jams.
A city of millions of scooters, where crossing the street is an extreme sport requiring absolute faith in destiny.
Vietnam’s southern heart, formerly Saigon, where a French baguette pairs perfectly with local pho soup.
A capital at the meeting point of three rivers, bearing the dark history of the Khmer Rouge and attracting visitors with the golden roofs of the Royal Palace.
A traffic-choked metropolis sinking so quickly that Indonesians have decided to build a new capital in the jungle.
Spanish forts, American malls and Asian jeepneys blended into one bubbling Filipino melting pot.
Home of the Petronas Twin Towers, where modern highways cut straight through tropical jungle.
A city-state where chewing gum litter can cost you a year’s budget, yet orchids bloom right in the airport.
A chaotic metropolis where sacred cows on the roads have higher priority than luxury sports cars.
The home of Bollywood and the Dharavi slums, a city of contrasts where millionaires live next door to street fortune-tellers.
India’s former British capital, preserving Victorian architecture and its reputation as the country’s most intellectual city.
A green, carefully planned city at the foot of the Himalayas, built specifically to be Pakistan’s ideal capital.
An ancient city encircled by harsh Afghan mountains, whose history is one long struggle for survival.
An oasis of glass and gold where you can ski in the scorching desert and buy a Bugatti from a vending machine.
The UAE capital that does not shout about its wealth but quietly displays the Louvre in the desert and the dazzling white Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque.
The heart of Saudi Arabia, where conservative traditions meet the construction of a mirrored futuristic megacity.
A Qatari oasis of skyscrapers and museums that became famous worldwide after Messi lifted the World Cup here.
An ancient city on seven hills, built of white stone, where Roman Theatre ruins sit beside an Eastern bazaar.
The Paris of the Middle East, destroyed and rebuilt so many times that its zest for life could make any European jealous.
One of the world’s oldest continuously inhabited cities, whose markets go back to biblical times.
A city of the Great Pyramids and insane traffic, where road rules are treated as mere suggestions.
Egypt’s maritime gateway, founded by Alexander the Great, where people now gaze across the Mediterranean instead of at the Pharos Lighthouse.
A city beneath Table Mountain, where penguins warm themselves on the beach and two oceans argue over whose storm is stronger.
South Africa’s administrative capital, turned purple in spring by thousands of blooming jacaranda trees.
The world capital of safari, where modern skyscrapers stand so close to the national park that giraffes peek into upper-floor windows.
Ethiopia’s capital and Africa’s diplomatic hub, where coffee is enjoyed for three hours as part of a sacred ritual.
A Nigerian giant and home of Nollywood, where population density and noise levels break every world record.
A city with a sail-like Opera House and a bridge everyone climbs for a selfie with a kangaroo.
A capital built as a compromise between Sydney and Melbourne so they would finally stop fighting over the title.
A cultural and coffee hub where the weather changes four times in fifteen minutes, making people wear shorts over a puffer jacket.
A city of sails and extinct volcanoes, where extras from The Lord of the Rings still drink ale in local pubs.
The world’s southernmost and windiest capital, where umbrellas break within three seconds of leaving the airport.
London’s murky artery, where royal swans glide elegantly while a couple of centuries of British secrets rest on the riverbed.
A Parisian waterway seemingly designed solely to reflect the lights of the Eiffel Tower and Alexander III Bridge.
Europe’s great cruise route, flowing through four capitals and collecting gossip in a dozen languages.
A hardworking river whose castles have seen so many knights and romantics that its water ought to taste of ale and poetry.
Italy’s largest river, feeding the Po Valley with rice for risotto and suffering droughts more often than Italians suffer from their own tempers.
The ancient sponsor of the Egyptian pharaohs; without it, the great civilization would have been little more than a very large pile of sand.
Africa’s deepest and most mysterious river, crossing the equator twice as if unable to decide which hemisphere it prefers.
The great American waterway where Tom Sawyer and Huckleberry Finn rafted toward adventure and American literature.
China’s Blue River, held back by the gigantic Three Gorges Dam, which can slow Earth’s rotation when the reservoir is full.
India’s sacred waters wash away the sins of millions of pilgrims and leave modern ecologists and microbiologists perplexed.
The river that gave its name to a whole civilization and country, then apparently took offense and moved to flow mostly through Pakistan.
A giant reservoir of the purest water, whose winter ice becomes the world’s most popular photo spot for bloggers.
Europe’s largest lake, whose unpredictable moods and storms historically made captains cross themselves before leaving port.
Lake. A northern mirror reflecting the wooden masterpieces of Kizhi, built without a single nail.
Lake. An African inland sea filled with thousands of endemic fish species, but with no truly safe swimming spots thanks to crocodiles.
Sea - The cradle of antiquity, separating resort-filled Europe, sightseeing-rich Asia and hot Africa.
Sea - A harsh northern body of water where swimming is not relaxation but a test of character and resistance to cold.
Sea - A paradise where pirates with rum have given way to tourists with piña coladas and enormous cruise ships.
The roof of the world, where mountains are so high that climbers pay thousands of dollars for the questionable pleasure of freezing on a summit.
European mountains where cows look cleaner than the average city dweller and ski resorts bankrupt people faster than casinos.
A natural wall where they make the proper shashlik, drink longevity-promoting kefir and argue about Mount Elbrus’s height.
The stone belt dividing the country into before and after, while supplying locals with tough character and malachite souvenirs.
The forested mountains of Eastern Europe, where tourists imagine Count Dracula’s castle behind every other tree.
The planet’s longest mountain range, where llamas serve as couriers and potatoes grow at dizzying heights.
A mountain chain stretching across two continents like a seam stitching the Americas from Alaska to Tierra del Fuego.
The planet’s highest peak, now the world’s highest and most expensive queue of people hoping to take a selfie.
The highest point in the Alps, ownership of which the French and Italians dispute as passionately as the recipe for the best cheese.
An Asian desert where, instead of classic sand, you find harsh rocks, icy winds and dinosaur bones.
A Turkmen desert famous for the Gates of Hell—a burning gas crater someone forgot to put out half a century ago.
Desert. The red sands of Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan, where camels roam among the dunes and archaeologists search for ancient Khwarezmian gold.
Desert. A place on Earth where it has not rained for so many centuries that local cacti have forgotten what roots are for.
A white silence at the top of the globe, where polar bears are the indigenous residents and polar explorers are their guests.
A vast region used to scare foreigners in movies and attract Russians with promises of Siberian health and cedar nuts.
A harsh southern land of drifting glaciers and storm winds, where penguins feel like masters of the universe.
The planet’s giant green lungs, breathing so heavily that they produce a fifth of all the oxygen on Earth.
A fish-shaped island where burdock leaves grow as tall as people and people eat spoonfuls of caviar more often than porridge.
A land of a thousand lakes and mosquitoes the size of sparrows, where the marble canyons of Ruskeala leave visitors speechless.
A land of geysers, volcanoes with complicated names and elves, in whom half the local population officially believes.
An island of unique evolution, where lemurs dance and baobabs look as if they were planted upside down.
A Ceylon tea paradise where elephants cross the road at zebra crossings and surfers chase waves from morning till night.
An island of high technology and night markets, making the world’s finest microchips and most delicious bubble tea.
A Mediterranean resort split in two, where cats outnumber people thanks to Saint Helena.
An Italian island with a Mafia past and smoking Mount Etna, where cannoli and oranges are the strongest arguments in any dispute.
A French island with a fiery Italian temperament that gave the world one very ambitious little emperor.
A tiny fortified island of the Knights, where Gladiator and Game of Thrones were filmed because the sets have been standing here since the age of chivalry.
New York’s concrete jungle, bought from Native Americans for a string of beads and now worth more than the rest of the planet combined.
Once Russian and now America’s largest state, where everyone searched for gold but mostly found permafrost.
A land of lederhosen, enormous beer mugs and fairy-tale castles built by Ludwig II, who clearly watched Disney before Disney existed.
A historic German region famous for porcelain, the Dresden Gallery and an extraordinarily difficult dialect.
A region in northern France where people drink cider and Calvados instead of wine, and Camembert smells so fierce it should be banned from the subway.
A French land of rugged cliffs and crêpes, where the tides put on a show twice a day.
Picturesque hills, cypress trees and Chianti wine that look exactly like your computer’s desktop wallpaper.
Italy’s wealthy north, where Milan makes what the world will wear next season and millionaires relax on Lake Como.
A proud autonomous region with Barcelona as its capital, dreaming of leaving Spain but not the football league.
The birthplace of flamenco and bullfighting, Spain’s hottest south, where the Moorish palaces of the Alhambra make you forget everything else.
A country where men wear skirts without embarrassment, drink Scotch and sincerely believe someone lives in Loch Ness.
Part of the United Kingdom where road signs look as if a cat walked across the keyboard (for example, Llanfairpwllgwyngyll).
A protected German wilderness where wolves and lynxes live so comfortably that anyone could envy them.
A US national park perched atop a supervolcano, entertaining tourists with geysers and terrifying scientists with the prospect of doomsday.
An attraction of a waterfall shared by Americans and Canadians so they can take tourists by boat beneath its icy spray.
Africa’s ‘Smoke That Thunders’, where the Zambezi plunges into a narrow gorge with such force that the spray can be seen 40 kilometres away.
Mount. Japan’s perfect snow-capped cone, which every self-respecting Japanese person should climb once—and only a fool would climb twice.
Mount. A volcano with a bad reputation that taught ancient Romans how quickly property with a mountain view can lose value.
An Inca city atop a mountain ridge that Spanish conquistadors never managed to find, while modern tourists have no trouble at all.
The most expensive and beautiful monument to eternal love, made of white marble, for which the emperor spared neither treasury nor architects.
A royal palace where gold, mirrors and fountains were meant to prove to subjects that Louis XIV’s taste came at a very high price.
Britain’s main alarm clock, which is actually a bell, though tourists stubbornly use the name for the entire clock tower.
Antiquity’s main amphitheatre, used by ancient Romans for gladiator fights and by modern Romans for selling souvenirs.
Athens’ sacred hill, restored for so long that the scaffolding around the Parthenon has practically become a historical monument itself.
A romantic city where water replaces asphalt, gondolas replace taxis and ordinary storm drains are in desperately short supply.
An open-air museum where so much art gives tourists Stendhal syndrome, while steak prices give them a heart attack.
The world’s fashion capital, where people dress as if they are about to walk onto a runway even when they are just buying bread.
The city of the Sagrada Família and Gaudí, where architecture resembles a frozen sandcastle and beaches are full of pickpockets.
A city of contrasts on two continents, where seagulls rule the Bosphorus and the streets belong to the world’s boldest, fattest cats.
Turkey’s main Mecca for all-inclusive fans, where Russian is heard more often than at resorts on Russia’s Black Sea coast.
An ancient city of three religions, where history is so concentrated that arguments over every stone have lasted for millennia.
A Thai island paradise where people come for endless summer, tom yum and the chance to ride a motorbike without a licence—until the first police patrol.
The world’s smallest and most overcrowded island capital, where the airport occupies an entire separate island among the Maldives.
Paris’s giant iron lady, built by Gustave Eiffel as a temporary structure but left forever to torment local aesthetes.
The world’s leading museum, where millions come for a three-minute selfie with the tiny Mona Lisa behind bulletproof glass.
Russia’s main museum, where you can walk 20 kilometres in a day, see the Peacock Clock and pet the famous Hermitage cats.
A kingdom of fountains outside St.Petersburg, where Samson tears open a lion’s jaws and hidden prank fountains drench unsuspecting tourists.
New York’s green lady welcomes immigrants with a torch, although the French originally gave her simply as a symbol of friendship.
The world’s tallest needle, piercing Dubai’s clouds and making tourists crane their necks while attempting vertical photos.
A body of water with extreme salinity where you cannot sink, but if the water gets into a scratch, you will discover every torment of hell.
Ocean. The planet’s largest and deepest ocean with destructive typhoons.
Ocean. The main water barrier between the Old and New Worlds, where people still search the seabed for Atlantis and the wreck of the Titanic.
Mount. Africa’s highest point, whose shining snowy cap in the middle of the savanna looks as if someone photoshopped it there.
A US national park where temperatures soar so high that shoe soles melt and rocks move around all by themselves out of boredom.
The deepest and darkest place on Earth, where sunlight never reaches but the pressure could flatten a tank like a pancake.
A giant crack in Arizona carved by the Colorado River over millions of years so people could have spectacular desktop wallpapers.
An island of eternal enlightenment, smoothie bowls and scooter crashes, where every second tourist suddenly becomes a life coach or investor.
A synonym for expensive, lazy holidays, where the whitest sand and turquoise water make your social media followers explode with envy.
A Thai resort island where elephants, beaches and night markets compete for tourists’ attention.
Spanish islands of eternal spring off the African coast, which became a symbol of outrageous wealth across the former Soviet Union in the 1990s.
An island where the music never stops until morning and the number of DJs per capita exceeds all reasonable limits.
A tiny atoll in French Polynesia where overwater bungalows cost so much that buying an apartment with a mortgage would be cheaper.
An African island of spices and white-sand beaches that gave the world the incomparable Freddie Mercury.
A US island state where everyone wears colourful shirts, dances the hula and surfs waves as tall as houses.
A huge Indonesian island home to tigers, orangutans and the world’s smelliest flower, the rafflesia.
The planet’s most populous island, which gave the world tonnes of excellent coffee and the name of a programming language.
A Russian metropolis where ‘I’m almost there’ means someone has only just stepped out of the shower and is assessing the scale of a three-hour traffic jam.
The cry someone makes after stepping barefoot on a LEGO brick in the dark.
A hot place where, according to a perfectionist, every font has been replaced with Comic Sans.
A taxi driver who can steer, count change and drink hot coffee at the same time.
A dance move attempted by someone slipping on an icy pavement in winter.
Something you desperately wish you could switch on retroactively, about two hours after an important argument ends.
A little cord with eyes that desperately wants to be mistaken for a fearsome viper.
That mysterious guy from school algebra whom everyone is always looking for, though nobody knows why.
The contents of a colleague’s tongue when she ‘just popped in to say hello’.
The place birds fly to at nature’s expense and people fly to on credit.
A natural cactus on legs that really dislikes having hard facts used against it.
The note that begins both a great symphony and the neighbour’s morning warm-up with a power drill.
The second note of the scale, forever feeling like the first note’s understudy.
A note that sounds proud but still finds itself somewhere in the middle.
A Chinese surname found on every third smartphone or every second programmer.
A voice message sent to a chat when all colleagues suddenly disappear for a lunch break that lasts a whole day.
The sound made as the last candy mysteriously disappears from the box marked ‘for tomorrow’.
An exclamation uttered when entering icy water or reading the electricity bill.
A programming language and the final note of the musical scale.
A melancholy little donkey, one of Christopher Robin’s friends, who was forever losing his tail.
Kipling’s wise python, who mastered hypnotism long before online gurus appeared.
A character from Greek mythology who wanted love so badly that he eventually fell in love with his own reflection in the water.
The wise sheep from the Shaun the Sheep cartoons, who always knows where the juiciest grass is growing.
The first syllable in the name of the bounciest tiger, who believed tigers were absolutely the best at everything.
The ancient Egyptian sun god, who staged an epic battle with the serpent Apep every evening instead of simply going to bed.
The Egyptian jackal-headed god who weighed sinners’ hearts and served as the strictest customs officer at the border of the afterlife.
The ibis-headed god of wisdom and writing, whose name in Russian sounds like the demonstrative pronoun for the guy standing over there.
The chief Egyptian judge of souls, who survived an extreme family dismemberment at the hands of his brother Set and still returned to work.
The ideal Egyptian wife and goddess of magic, who literally pieced her husband Osiris back together, giving a masterclass in marital devotion.
The cat-headed goddess of joy, worshipped by ancient Egyptians as fervently as modern internet users worship cats on social media.
The Egyptian god of the desert and fury, who became history’s worst brother by giving Osiris an unforgettable coffin-based ‘quest’.
The chief Greek god, whose lightning bolts were work tools and endless affairs were his main hobby.
The Greek ruler of the underworld, owner of the gloomiest real estate and the most loyal three-headed guard dog.
The Greek god of war, who loved picking fights but became terribly fussy and complained to Dad Zeus whenever he got wounded himself.
A winged Greek troublemaker with a bow who shot without warning and made respectable gods behave like lovesick teenagers.
The Greek god of trade and theft, who invented winged sandals long before sports brands started making cushioned sneakers.
Jupiter’s moon with the shortest name and the most explosive temperament, where volcanoes smoke without a lunch break.
Saturn’s moon, wrapped in such a dense orange atmosphere that astronomers struggled for ages to spot its methane lakes.
A moon of Mars whose name means ‘Fear’, although it looks like a frightened, oddly shaped space potato.
The smaller moon of Mars, symbolizing ‘Terror’, orbiting beside its brother Phobos to the delight of astronomy fans.
Pluto’s moon, so huge compared with its host that the two dance through space like equal partners.
Jupiter’s moon, hiding its entire ocean beneath such a thick crust of ice that scientists still dream of drilling a fishing hole.
The largest moon in the Solar System, which managed to outgrow even the planet Mercury.
Saturn’s moon, constantly ‘sneezing’ powerful geysers of ice and vapour into space and feeding its planet’s rings.
Neptune’s moon, moving backwards along its orbit and showing the stubbornest, most rebellious attitude among major moons.
Earth’s only natural satellite, forever showing us just one side while keeping all its secrets hidden.
A Belgian village that became shorthand for the crushing finale of one very ambitious French emperor in a bicorne hat.
A Greek settlement that gave its name to the 42-kilometre race thanks to one very hurried messenger with good news.
The city near which King Charles XII of Sweden learned first-hand that winter holidays in Russia are not the best idea.
A village near Moscow where Russians and French exchanged such grand ‘courtesies’ that Napoleon ended up occupying an empty Moscow.
An ancient Apulian village where Hannibal gave the Romans a masterclass in tactical encirclement that haunted the legions.
An ancient city whose security team made history’s stupidest mistake by accepting a huge wooden horse as a gift from the enemy.
A French city whose outskirts saw such a gigantic and pointless slaughter in World War I that it was called ‘the mill’.
An Italian castle where the German emperor had to walk barefoot through the snow just to tell the Pope, ‘Sorry, I was wrong.
A small river that Julius Caesar crossed before realizing the bridges were burned, the die was cast and there was no way back to the Senate.
A luxurious suburb of Paris where kings bathed in gold and, in the twentieth century, the Germans had to sign a peace treaty they deeply disliked.
An ancient Roman resort whose residents realized too late that the mountain on the horizon was not a pretty backdrop but an active volcano.
A Crimean resort where Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill divided the post-war world over tea as confidently as if they were playing a board game.
A German city where former leaders of the Reich faced the strictest and fairest verdict from an international tribunal after the war.
A Paris fortress-prison that furious French citizens dismantled brick by brick to show the king exactly what they thought of his absolutism.
Islands at the edge of the world over which Argentina and Britain somehow managed to wage a small but full-scale naval war in the early 1980s.
The strait where the Russian fleet suffered such a crushing defeat by the Japanese in 1905 that it entered the textbooks of naval tactics forever.
A Greek island off whose coast the cunning Themistocles lured the huge Persian fleet into a narrow strait and gave King Xerxes a historic thrashing.
A narrow mountain pass where 300 Spartans under Leonidas staged the most expensive and furious delay in the history of military logistics.
A region where the nineteenth-century Gold Rush was so intense that thousands of men left their families to wash dirt in the hope of becoming millionaires.
The lost Inca city high in the Andes that Spanish conquistadors somehow failed to notice, preserving it for millions of future tourists.
An ancient Roman amphitheatre where gladiators fought to the death for free entertainment and the good mood of a fickle crowd.
An ancient fortified hill in Athens that survived Persians, Turks and Venetian bombardment, and still proudly supports the ruined Parthenon.
A suburb of Berlin where, in the summer of 1945, the victorious powers finalized Europe’s new borders to avoid repeating old mistakes.
The capital of a great empire whose mighty walls fell to Sultan Mehmed’s giant cannons in 1453, closing an entire chapter of medieval history.
An ancient hero who hacked the mythical system perfectly: he reflected Medusa’s gaze in a mirrored shield and removed her head without harming himself.
The heavyweight champion of ancient Greece, forced to complete twelve brutal contracts for the cowardly King Eurystheus, including cleaning the Augean stables.
An Athenian lad who proved that knowing how to unwind a ball of thread in the Minotaur’s home is far more important than simply swinging a sword well.
The clever king of Ithaca who came up with the wooden-horse startup at Troy, then spent ten years getting home from work and collecting every possible travel mishap along the way.
The superhero of the Trojan War, almost invulnerable, who fell victim to an annoying security-system bug in his heel.
The ancient leader of an extreme cruise aboard the Argo, who set off for the Golden Fleece but ended up with a heap of problems involving his new girlfriend Medea.
History’s first amateur aviator, who ignored safety rules and his father’s instructions by flying too close to the sun on wax wings.
A virtuoso musician whose voice could make even stones weep, but who failed the simplest quest—‘don’t look back’—while leading his beloved wife out of Hades.
The Sun’s closest neighbour, spinning so fast that its year lasts just three months, while daytime temperatures could melt even the toughest kitchen Teflon.
The Solar System’s infernal frying pan, disguised as a beautiful morning star but hiding lead-melting temperatures and sulfuric acid rain beneath its clouds.
The Solar System’s heavyweight and Earth’s cosmic shield, acting like a giant vacuum cleaner for passing comets while showing off its Great Red Spot, a giant storm.
Space’s ultimate fashionista, never leaving its orbit without its luxurious collection of hat brims made of billions of icy crumbs and cosmic dust.
An ice giant that decided to be different and rolls around the Sun completely on its side, inspiring astronomers to joke about its extremely lazy behaviour.
